posts.body_html:
bogman, totally missed your question!

Yes, these do get fertilizer, but sparingly. I fertilize them with maxsea, 1/4 strength, 1X per month only during the fall and spring when the plants are in active vegetative growth. If you fertilize them too often during this time, they'll grow very big and fat, but as soon as it heats up, they'll almost all perish! Slow and steady is one of the keys to keeping them alive long term, and I suspect this is why I've lost most of my clones over time. Since these are so rot prone, it's a balancing act to feed them enough to get some nice sized blooms and replacement tubers for the next year, yet not too much such that they become susceptible to rot when the weather changes.

I don't like using hardcore chemical fungicides, which has been my achille's heel with Disas. I'd probably have much better success spraying the crap out of these all the time. As a middle ground, I've sprayed them with dusting sulfur (mixed in water) every once in a while, and put sulfur on any spots that look like disease. It has worked quite well so far. The disease usually shows up in the winter months when it's rainy and cloudy for weeks on end and during the summer when it gets over 100F around here.


Regarding flower shelf life, if kept on the plant and in a cool area, I've had flowers last over 1.5 months, it's crazy! This is sorta misleading though, I'm talking about the life of the entire spike with multiple blooms, not an individual flower. Main issue in flower shelf life is thrips, other insects, slugs, snails, and even sunburn if you're risky like me. If you have them in a greenhouse, you proably won't have the challenges I have.

You're spot on: they are growing with the wasabi, but with a few more hours of filtered sunlight. Correction: the sunlight is direct when it's cold outside, but filtered when it warms up.

posts.body_html:
Well, at this stage in my Disa life, I've lost almost every single plant except maybe 4 clones. With whatever was left, I repotted most of them in fresh, homegrown Sphaghnum moss with the hopes of building up another nice collection. The clones that are left have survived neglect, top soil being spilled on them, heat waves, multiple cases of fungal rot, poor water quality, and probably excess fertilizing (accidently). without a doubt, the remaining clones are very special and are much more resilient than all other disa clones that I've grown in the past.


It took about 6 hours to do these 3 small trays! Why does it take so long? Separating disas is difficult, cleaning them equally difficult, and the roots/tubers are more fragile than thin glass! Planting in stringy sphagnum isn't the easiest either, as you have to be careful not to snap the roots when you push the moss down. It looks really easy to do, but it's harder than you think to get them centered and potted up at the right height. I probabaly potted some of these a little too shallow, but we'll see, maybe that's a good thing to have the "stem" exposed to less soil.



Another shot, and yes, that heliamphora stays outdoors all year round!


And a blast from the past, orchids that I used to grow well that are all now in plant heaven...well, maybe in hell because of what they put me through LOL

These seedlings went from tiny to almost blooming size in about 9 months! Of course, every last one of them died about a month after this photo was taken, never got to see what the flowers looked like:

posts.body_html:
Disas are notorious for being susceptible to fungal diseases. I've killed every last disa I've ever grown minus 4 different clones, and the puzzle of preventing rot has really sparked my interest into this plant again! Most people would be like "EF that! Why try?" To be honest, I probably have psychological issues, those flowers are just so damn beautiful.

I've always read that with disas, you'll have to use fungicides if you want to grow them successfully, and in my climate, that's probably true. If you live in an area that stays cool all year round, then you probably won't have to. Anytime they are stressed, they are vulnerable.

Not many disa growers go into details about their failures, but I believe that killing plants is the only way to really know how to grow one! Here's some ways to manage rot on disas:
1) Transplant every fall.
2) bottom water! This will help prevent rot on the leaves and stems, but this won't remedy root rot.
3) Give the plants a lot of time to recover from transplanting before fertilizing with very dilute fertilizer.
4) If you saw mild symptoms of rot on a plant when transplanting, it probably can't be fertilized until that rot disappears or is no longer on the plant. Fertilizer turns rot into a wildfire, even when in low concentrations!
5) plants grown slow and steady are more resistant to disease than plants pumped up like Arnold Schwartznegger.
6) most clones are just susceptible to rot, but some have higher resistance. breeding the resistant ones is the way to go!
7)Grow away from woodchips or other decomposing material that can sporulate. Cement floors or inorganic surroundings are best. I learned this the hard way: in my previous grow site, all my disas grew on cement, so rot wasn't as bad. I grew them this time with woodchips under the trays, and afternoon pure shade+lots of watering+woodchips=disaster.
8)So far, I've been able to beat rot by moving them into a makeshift shelter that is located in full sun. The shelter has 75% shade, so the plants get bright, indirect light all day long. Bright, indirect light, along with great air circulation makes all the difference in the world, but it won't necessarily stop rot. Along with changing the envionment, I added copious amounts of sulfur to all infected parts of the plant. In some cases, I was too late and lost the main plant, but hopefully the side shoots will survive:




In this case below, I applied sulfur on the rotting stem and beat it! How do I know that I won the battle(at least temporarily)? Stems turn totally brown on disas in a matter of 2-3 days. This sulfur was applied 2 weeks ago, so without a doubt, this plant made it because it's still alive. The hope is the rot doesn't come back later on!


Below are pictures of the new makeshift shelter with the shade cloth taken off so you can see the plants!







A pot that hasn't been transplanted in 2 years. If the soil breaks down too much, the roots will turn brown, and that can lead to stem/tuber rot. Interestingly, the roots on this plant are in perfect shape since the sphagnum hasn't broken down enough. Properly dried and stored home grown sphaghnum might last longer than the wild collected stuff:

posts.body_html:
Your dedication (polite word for a mutually-shared obsession with plants) is honorable! Perhaps you'll be surrounded by Disas in the after life!

Have you tried Actinovate, Trichoderma, or any of the other biofungicides? Yeah, they aren't cheap, but should store in the fridge for a year or two and might help, especially when the plants are stressed. Here's a handy info sheet from UMass. That's one of the best fact sheets I've seen.

I've used some of these with good success, helping crops like parsley survive during crazy rains and humidity. Some of the biofungicides can tolerate sulfur, but others may be adversely affected. Since any use would begin at planting/replanting, if you needed sulfur, it would indicate the bio control agent wasn't effective anyway. I'd make a wild guess that Gliocladium catenulatum or Trichoderma would be the most helpful, since they attack a lot of soil borne pathogens, the most common ones.

posts.body_html:
I haven't tried trichoderma, but that's a great suggestion! Some hardcore chemicals that will shrink your you know what was purchased a few weeks ago for my Yoinashi asian pear (sprayed during dormancy only), so I might experiment with using this stuff on a few of the disas to see how effective it is.

It seems anytime you have fungal pathogens attacking your plants, something is off with the environment. So far, as long as the infected area is completely doused in sulfur, the plant will survive. You can't dissolve it in water and spray it on, it's just not concentrated enough-rot will still take over. The infected area literally needs to be dusted with sulfur as shown in some of the pics above. If you wash that off, even weeks later, the pathogen can come back and kill the plant!

Right now, we have relatively luke warm winter temps (low 60's during the day, high 50's at night), very high humidity, botrytis spores EVERYWHERE after our first rain, somewhat stagnant air, and more rain in the forecast. I haven't watered the disas for 2 weeks now, and every time you water, you risk killing plants, as the moisture gives the fungal pathogens a chance to take over.

The winter strategy is to keep the plants out of rain, keep them frost free, keep the grow area dry as possible, give them as much bright, indirect light as possible, and only water them on sunny, dry days. The substrate is borderline dry right now, but not dry enough to kill or stress the plants. The next watering will be done in the morning and I'll remove the shade cloth so they're hit with full sun all day, but just that one day.

Moving them to full sun at this time of year has proven a winning strategy, but they do need shade cloth because too many sunny days in a row will lead to purpling of the leaves (which is stressful for the plants). If I were to fertilize them right now, I'd probabably lose half of the plants, so despite nice growth right now, I have to wait until the weather changes and there's no chance of fungal outbreaks. The tubers should have plenty of food to keep them going for now.

If you're a disa grower, take notes, this info is gold. Most other growers won't tell you these details.

posts.body_html:
Well, Meizz.,

Ya aint s'pose ta put the fungicides on your "you know what", even if it looks like a fungus!

Once the pathogen is present, suppression is only a short-term fix, since the spores are lurking, hiding, waiting 

I knew an orchid grower who watered all his orchids with diluted quat. salts; I think it was Physan 20. I'm fairly sure it'll kill sphagnum, but live moss may not be necessary. The Subdue/Zyban or Cleary's 336 mix would likely clear it up, but you'd want to sanitize the plants, wash, and disinfect the pots, area, etc. Then, there's your "wiilie"" concerns!

A lot of plants grown here get rot issues if the stem or foliage gets wet. Bottom water here almost always ends up in death, because the media saturates, fills to holding capacity. For plants like Cephalotus, which is highly susceptible to Botrytis, I keep moss pulled away from the stems and water two corners of the pot, away from the crown. That way, the media gets moist, but not wet, and the stem area is last to get moisture, so it's drier. With many plants, as long as the distal roots are moist, the plant is happy. Sulcorebutia rauschii violacidermis is famous for rot, so the top media is pumice/gravel and the organics near the root tips; it's watered in one corner of the pot, seasonally.

If, on the other hand, Disas need wet media, maybe dropping the pH would help. Dave Parkinson, in the UK, uses 60% peat and 40% perlite. He claims to have had problems with sphagnum. It's colder there, so, who knows?

Do Disas have a velamen, like other orchids? In terrestrials, like Calopogon, it's thinner than in in epiphytes, but it's there. If so, there's a clue, since velamen tissues absorb water vapor, vs. water film. Pathogens love water film; nasty little zoospores swimming towards destruction.

So much to consider! And, you've made marvelous progress.

My orchid goal, quest, ...thing, is Dendrophylax lindenii (Polyrrhiza l.) I'm on the lookout for some Mockernut hickory bark slabs, before attempting to acquire some starts. I'm thinking it would survive(?) in the Nepenthes greenhouse, inside a humidity tube made of Kalwall. Still, it has one of the worst reputations for growing/thriving in the plant world! Yay!

posts.body_html:
It's been a tough ride this year for the disas. Almost every last plant has some amount of fungal attack on it. Under my current conditions and given the time of year, anytime you water these plants, you risk losing them.

The "new" plants I acquired in late October of this year all came with a disease that wasn't present in my collection, so now I'm learning how to control this new disease. Looking back, disas weren't this difficult to grow, so my conclusion is that once you get a disease, it's always there, it never goes away. Only way to get rid of it is to get rid of your collection, clean the environment out, and start over with material grown in vitro. Even that, over time, you'll probably get a new disease showing up eventually, so conquering Disas is all about mitigating disease.

Well, here they are in early December, I'm dreading watering them again. However, the sulfur technique is working like a charm, haven't lost anything in a while:

Even that, over time, you'll probably get a new disease showing up eventually, so conquering Disas is all about mitigating disease.
Pathogens, bah humbug! Yes, spores float or can splash, wash in, or arrive on the butt of a frog .

The presence of the pathogen is either growing or resting (spores, sclerotia, etc.) or both. The resting stages are the most difficult to control, but easier to mechanically remove by washing, discarding media, disinfectants, et al. The only other alternative is to use fungicides. These can either attack spores/resting stages, as is often the case with Mancozeb, or the germinating spores get attacked, which may be what the sulfur is doing. Sulfur could also kill active fungi if damaged tissues allow osmotic absorption. It could also be lowering the pH outside of the pathogen's tolerance range.

Once you see damage, chances are the fungus is now inside the plant tissue(s). At this stage, suppression is a time bomb. Your choices are: to pitch the plant(s) or infected plant parts (e.g. leaves), change the environment to a point where the pathogen dies off because it cannot tolerate the environment, establish a biological control, or use systemic fungicides.

Eventually, if the pathogen is suppressed long enough, it can die off. I was given some Heliamphora, years ago, with Phytophthora showing up shortly after potting them up. Situation: systemic infection with unknown spore, zoospore status.

Remedy: Isolate infected plants. Treat with Subdue fungicide to halt or kill disease. After a week, when pathogen is pretty much static or dead, put on nitrile gloves, move plants outdoors, to a remote area and discard soil, wash plants and pots, remove infected areas, as possible, and toss the pots into a 10% bleach solution. Carefully remove gloves and trash them. This will greatly reduce or eliminate any resting stages, especially if cleaning is thorough. As the fungicide has suppressed or killed the pathogen, new spores aren't being generated. The cycle is disrupted.

The original growing area was sprayed with disinfectants: first Greenshield (quat. salts); after drying, some hours later, 10% bleach. Never mix the aforementioned disinfectants. Follow all label directions.

Freshly repotted plants were returned to the original growing area, vs. risking spreading the problem. Plants were treated regularly with systemic fungicides for about eight months. After that time, I stopped treatment and kept an eye on the plants. It has now been over ten years without the pathogen and fungicides aren't used unless I'm overdue to repot and the plants are very crowded, a precautionary measure.

This was a lot of work, but Heliamphora were very rare and valuable at the time, not easily replaced. The point is it is possible to get rid the pathogen. Without fungicides, the challenge is great. A biological fungicide, or group of these, may be useful. I'd experiment on some spare plants, to determine tolerance to disinfectant quat. salts, which many orchids tolerate. That can help eliminate resting stages, germinating spores and surface infections. Figure disinfectants will kill sphagnum. If the plants can tolerate being bare rooted and soaked in disinfectant, at least you know the plant's surface will likely be clean. After this, or a regular wash and repot, that would be the time to start introducing biologicals.

If stem infections are the principal infection site, I'd start there. Pull moss away from the stem, crown and replace it with something which dries out quickly or does not stay as wet. Do you keep the stem and foliage dry when watering? Many rabbit holes you have. Many questions there are.

posts.body_html:
It used to be that only the leaves and stems got infected, but with the new pathogen, now the roots get infected as well.
Yes, plants are bottom watered only, and they're under greenhouse plastic, so they never get rained on. Top of soil is slightly moist, but barely. New plants don't share same trays as the old plants to prevent spread of the new pathogen, but it might spread anyways via becoming airborn. Good point, with hardcore fungicides, you can probably eventually get rid of these pathogens. I use 3ppm water on these just to be sure salt isn't an issue.

We'll see, I'm debating trying to avoid using hardcore chemical fungicides and see if I can grow these with just sulfur applications. In the past, I got the fungal disease and didn't use ANY fungicides EVER for many years. It wouldn't ever get bad enough, although I did lose plants here and there, but I wouldn't have massive outbreaks like I'm seeing now. In the old environment, the same pathogen was manageable, it didn't kill the plants a few days after infecting them. Today, if you don't stop the pathogen, the plant is dead within 2-3 days.

I wasn't half as careful growing these plants on pavement at my old place, and they did 4X better there. Being surrounded by rotting woodchips all year round makes it an uphill battle at the new site. I had a pot that hadn't been watered in 2 weeks, yet both of the side shoots started rotting maybe 1-2 days before. The top of the soil was starting to get dry, and it was moist underneath, this is how I know that the soil moisture level isn't the problem. I've never been so frustrated in my life growing plants, sometimes you have to throw up the flag until you can provide the right conditions. Sarracenias are like weeds compared to these plants....

posts.body_html:
The wood chips may be upping the humidity, but it's unlikely it's harboring pathogens, unless they're washed-in and just sitting there. Saprophytes tend to colonize chips and many are antagonistic to pathogens. It's possible slugs or insects in the mulch (e.g.Collembola) can move around spores. But there may be another cultural element to consider: concrete tends to get colder at night and has almost no insulating value. The best high elevation Heliamphora I grew, years ago, were pots sitting on cold concrete.

A fast kill time smacks of Phytophthora, doesn't it? Since at least one, if not two pathogens have set up shop there, I'd go with the fungicides. The trusty Zyban (1 TBS/gal) + Subdue (7-8 drops/gal.) might be a good experiment. You could do better by separating the chemicals, Subdue drench and Zyban "sprench". Follow that 24 hours later with a pure water flush. Test a couple spares/duplicates first. These will work best over 65 degrees F, 70-75 F would be perfect. If the plants improve, repeat a couple times (about every 4 weeks), carefully wash and repot on normal cycle, sanitize the area when you repot and introduce biologicals after repotting. At that point, the pathogen(s) may be gone or greatly diminished. Email me if that's a path you wish to explore.

Sarracenia often have a startling quantity of endophytes, biologicals woven between intercellular tissues. Plus, their temperature tolerances, frozen to 120 F+ means some of their season is spent outside most pathogens' comfort zone. Full sun (UV) tends to waste a lot of spores, too. Might be interesting to see if the Sarracenia endophytes can cross over into Disas; you never know!

Instead of bottom watering, maybe watering 2-3 corners, away from the crown, would be better. The thicker and longer-lasting a water film is, the easier it is for many pathogens to spread and establish. In our climate, for example, bottom watering often leads to mature Sarracenia death. As a crazy humid, historically agricultural region (since before Thomas Jefferson), humans built a nauseating assortment of pathogens into the environment. Fortunately, microbes that eat pathogens are also present. In the war of microbes, it's often small tweaks in culture that favor one or more of the combatants.
